0.0.n: This is the philosopher's name, written in katakana.

0.1.n: は introduces Wittgenstein as the topic of the sentence.

0.3.n: 日常 connects to the following description through の.

0.4.n: の links everyday life to the various relationships being discussed.

0.5.n: 様々 needs な before a noun such as 関係性.

0.6.n: な lets 様々 describe the following noun.

0.7.n: 関係性 emphasizes connections or relations rather than individual things.

0.8.n: の links 関係性 to 中, forming the idea of being within relationships.

0.9.n: 中 refers to an abstract setting here, not a physical interior.

0.10.n: で marks the setting where the splitting occurs.

0.11.n: 言語 refers to language generally, not one particular language.

0.12.n: の links language to its meaning.

0.13.n: 意味 is what splits into multiple forms in this clause.

0.14.n: が identifies 意味 as what undergoes the splitting.

0.15.n: 複数 indicates more than one, contrasting with a single unified meaning.

0.16.n: に marks the resulting state after 分裂する.

0.17.n: 分裂する is the plain form, describing what happens before こと turns the clause into a noun.

0.18.n: こと turns the preceding description into something that can be discussed as a noun.

0.19.n: を marks the whole process as what Wittgenstein described.

0.21.n: 言語 combines with ゲーム to form a philosophical term.

0.22.n: ゲーム is an English borrowing; here it forms part of Wittgenstein's term 言語ゲーム.

0.24.n: と marks the wording used to describe the preceding process.

0.25.n: 表現しました is the polite past form of 表現する.

1.0.n: そして connects this statement to the previous explanation.

1.2.n: 言語 is discussed as a general concept here.

1.3.n: は sets language as the topic of the first clause.

1.4.n: 完全 combines with に to describe the degree of independence.

1.5.n: に turns 完全 into a description of how independently language exists.

1.6.n: 独立して is the て-form of 独立する, describing the state in which something exists.

1.7.n: 存在する is the plain form before こと.

1.8.n: こと turns 存在する and its modifiers into a noun phrase.

1.9.n: は highlights independent existence as what is not possible.

1.10.n: できず is a written-style negative linking form of できる, continuing the sentence rather than ending it.

1.12.n: あらゆる directly precedes a noun and includes every possible kind.

1.13.n: 言語 is modified by あらゆる to include every kind of language.

1.14.n: は introduces all language as the topic of the next clause.

1.15.n: 言語 forms the first part of the compound 言語ゲーム.

1.16.n: ゲーム forms part of the philosophical term, rather than referring to an ordinary recreational game.

1.17.n: の connects 言語ゲーム to 中 to express being inside its context.

1.18.n: 中 describes an abstract framework here rather than a physical space.

1.19.n: で marks the setting in which language is used.

1.20.n: 使用される is the passive form of 使用する: language receives the action rather than performing it.

1.21.n: こと turns 使用される into a noun phrase that can connect to で.

1.22.n: で marks being used as the means by which language gains meaning.

1.23.n: 初めて emphasizes that meaning arises only once the stated condition is met.

1.24.n: 意味 combines with 持つ to describe language having significance.

1.25.n: を marks 意味 as what language has.

1.26.n: 持つ means possessing something abstract here, rather than physically holding an object.

1.27.n: と marks the preceding claim as the content of Wittgenstein's position.

1.28.n: した is the past form of する; とした here reports a position someone adopted.

1.29.n: の adds an explanatory tone to the preceding statement before です.

1.30.n: です makes the explanatory ending のです polite.

2.0.n: 日常 directly modifies 言語 as part of the compound 日常言語.

2.1.n: 言語 combines with 日常 to refer to language used in ordinary life.

2.2.n: を marks everyday language as what is being understood.

2.3.n: 理解する is the plain form before ため, expressing the intended goal.

2.4.n: ため follows a plain verb to introduce a goal in the pattern ために.

2.5.n: に completes ために, which introduces the purpose of an action.

2.6.n: は highlights that purpose as the topic for stating what is necessary.

2.8.n: 言語 combines with ゲーム to name the philosophical concept discussed earlier.

2.9.n: ゲーム completes the term 言語ゲーム, whose rules are the focus here.

2.10.n: の links the language-game to its rules.

2.11.n: ルール is an English borrowing; Japanese does not mark it as singular or plural.

2.12.n: を marks the rules as what must be grasped.

2.13.n: 把握する refers to mentally understanding something, not physically grabbing it.

2.14.n: こと turns grasping the rules into a noun phrase.

2.15.n: が marks grasping the rules as what is necessary.

2.16.n: 必要 states a requirement and is followed by polite です.

2.17.n: です gives the statement a polite ending.

0.lit: Wittgenstein described language's meaning splitting into multiple forms within various everyday relationships as language-games.
0.tip: The pattern AをBと表現する means to describe A as B.

1.lit: Furthermore, language cannot exist completely independently; he held that all language has meaning only through being used within language-games.
1.tip: ことで初めて means only through doing something, emphasizing a necessary condition rather than a first occasion.

2.lit: To understand everyday language, grasping the language-game's rules is necessary.
2.tip: Aするためには、Bが必要です means that B is necessary in order to do A.
